analysis.one_liner: Caps Medicare drug plan premium increases and orders the government to negotiate drug prices for seniors.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: introduced in February 2008 with no cosponsors, it was sent to two House committees and died there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would do two things for the roughly 25 million Medicare beneficiaries in the Part D prescription drug program. First, it would cap how much drug plans could raise their bids — the costs that flow into beneficiaries' premiums — to no more than the annual Social Security cost-of-living increase [S3]. Second, it would delete the 2003 Medicare law's 'noninterference' clause, which barred the government from negotiating with drug companies, and instead direct the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates on behalf of Medicare drug plans [S3]. The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees and referred to the Health subcommittee, and never received any further action before the Congress ended in January 2009 [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D beneficiaries, whose premiums would no longer rise faster than their Social Security checks, and taxpayers, who fund a large share of Part D costs and would benefit if the government paid lower negotiated prices for prescription drugs [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps annual increases in Medicare Part D plan bids to the Social Security cost-of-living percentage, effective for plan years beginning January 1, 2009, so premiums would not outgrow seniors' Social Security benefits.

Strikes the Medicare law's 'noninterference' provision and requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with pharmaceutical manufacturers for drugs covered under Part D plans and Medicare Advantage drug plans.
Requires the Secretary to report to Congress every six months on the negotiations and the price reductions achieved, creating public accountability for the results.
Preserves existing formulary access rules and allows private plans to still seek discounts below the negotiated price, so plans could not argue negotiation would reduce drug coverage choices.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose prices and rebates for Medicare-covered drugs would be negotiated by the government instead of set through private deals, and Medicare drug plan insurers, whose annual bid growth would be capped by the cost-of-living ceiling [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill's negotiation mandate is open-ended: it requires the Secretary to negotiate but sets no price target, enforcement mechanism, or remedy if companies refuse to concede meaningful discounts, so critics in 2008 argued it could produce negotiations with little actual price reduction.

Capping plan bids to the Social Security cost-of-living increase, which excludes medical inflation, could squeeze plans if actual drug costs grow faster than the COLA, potentially leading to reduced coverage, higher cost-sharing, or plans exiting the market.
The premium cap is soft: it only prevents a plan's bid from exceeding the prior bid plus the COLA percentage, and the bill includes no additional penalty beyond that limit for plans that exceed it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — government negotiation of Medicare drug prices — is substantial for beneficiaries and taxpayers, since Medicare is the nation's largest prescription drug purchaser and had been barred by the 2003 law from using that buying power. The premium cap is blunter and could pressure plans where drug costs outpace the Social Security COLA. On balance, the potential savings outweigh the design risks, but the bill was never seriously developed: it drew no cosponsors and no committee action, so it never faced scrutiny that could have fixed its weaknesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and to the Health subcommittee on February 7, 2008, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Wexler introduced the Medicare Prescription Drug Affordability Act of 2008 in the House on February 7, 2008.
No member of the House cosponsored the bill.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee, and then referred to the Health subcommittee, where its action history ends.
The bill received no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote in the 110th Congress, which ended January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and the private insurers that sell Medicare Part D drug plans are better off: the government remained barred from negotiating drug prices under the 2003 Medicare law, and plan bids and premiums continued to rise without a cost-of-living ceiling. Medicare beneficiaries gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmaceutical makers and Part D insurers

for.name: Rep. Robert Wexler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral but took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, and with zero cosponsors the bill's support was limited to its single Democratic sponsor, so no partisan pattern can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would replace the 2003 law's 'noninterference' clause with a mandate that the government negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates for Medicare-covered drugs, ending drug makers' guarantee that Washington would not use its purchasing power. Medicare is the largest single drug purchaser in the country, so negotiated prices would cut into the industry's highest-margin sales. The bill died, so the industry kept its protection.

industries.industry: Health insurers selling Medicare Part D and Medicare Advantage drug plans
industries.note: Capping plan bids to the Social Security cost-of-living increase limits how much these plans can grow their premiums, while the negotiation mandate could lower their drug acquisition costs. In practice the insurers benefit from the status quo: the bill that would constrain them never advanced.
